title: The philosophy of Open Knowledge
description: A rigorous journey through twenty-seven centuries of giving knowledge away — from the Library of Alexandria and the Encyclopédie to public libraries, free software, Wikipedia and open access — and how Open Knowledge deliberately joins that tradition.

questions.text: What did the library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh demonstrate about libraries?

choices.text: That collections should be reserved for kings and priests
That a library can carry knowledge across a gap of time no single life could bridge
That clay tablets were superior to papyrus

questions.explanation: Texts like the Epic of Gilgamesh survived two and a half millennia of oblivion because they had been collected: the library outlived its civilization and delivered its knowledge to ours.

questions.text: What was the defining ambition of the Library of Alexandria?

choices.text: To collect all knowledge and make it available to working scholars
To protect Egyptian state secrets
To sell copies of scrolls to visiting merchants

questions.explanation: Alexandria tried to collect everything and functioned as a workshop, not a vault — scholars like Euclid and Eratosthenes worked beside the stacks. Its lesson: a sealed library is a tomb; an open one is an engine.

questions.text: What made Diderot and d'Alembert's Encyclopédie radical in the eighteenth century?

choices.text: Its premise that all knowledge, organized and explained, belonged in the hands of anyone who could read
It was the first book printed with movable type
It rejected the documentation of practical trades and crafts

questions.explanation: The Encyclopédie documented crafts alongside philosophy and aimed, in Diderot's words, 'to change the common way of thinking'. Authorities censored it precisely because open knowledge redistributes power.

questions.text: Why did Carnegie place the free library first among the worthy uses of a fortune?

choices.text: Because a library helps only those willing to help themselves — it rewards exactly the effort a learner brings, and nothing else
Because books were the cheapest goods to donate
Because libraries generated rental income for the town

questions.explanation: In The Gospel of Wealth (1889) Carnegie argued that 'the man who dies thus rich dies disgraced' and championed free libraries — funding more than 2,500, on condition that each community commit to operating theirs.

questions.text: Which principle did the nineteenth-century public library movement establish?

choices.text: Access to knowledge should not depend on wealth — libraries free at the point of use, funded as a public good
Reading rooms should charge a small entry fee to ensure seriousness
Libraries should record what every citizen reads

questions.explanation: From the UK Public Libraries Act (1850) to Boston — founded 1848, 'Free to All' over its door — societies began funding free libraries for everyone, with an ethic of reader privacy that long predates digital privacy debates.

questions.text: What does Baghdad's House of Wisdom illustrate about how knowledge survives?

choices.text: Knowledge moves because institutions choose to move it, and pay the cost gladly
Knowledge survives only in its original language
Translation corrupts knowledge and should be avoided

questions.explanation: The Abbasid translation movement paid to bring Greek, Persian and Indian science into Arabic — preserving works Europe had lost and adding algebra and algorithms along the way.

questions.text: Which of these is one of free software's four freedoms?

choices.text: The freedom to study how a program works and change it
The freedom to use software without ever paying taxes
The freedom to keep modifications secret forever

questions.explanation: Stallman's four freedoms are: run for any purpose, study and change (source required), redistribute copies, and distribute modified versions. 'Free as in freedom, not as in free beer.'

questions.text: What is copyleft, as introduced by the GNU GPL?

choices.text: Using copyright law to require that derivative works remain free — the gift protects itself
The abolition of copyright for software
A registry where authors renounce attribution

questions.explanation: The GPL grants the four freedoms but requires derivatives to carry the same license. It turned copyright — the tool of enclosure — into a mechanism that keeps the commons open.

questions.text: What did Elinor Ostrom's Governing the Commons demonstrate?

choices.text: Communities can govern shared resources sustainably — the 'tragedy of the commons' is a failure of governance, not a law of nature
All shared resources inevitably collapse
Only state ownership can protect common goods

questions.explanation: Ostrom's decades of field evidence earned the 2009 Nobel in Economics, just as Linux and Wikipedia were proving her point at planetary scale.

questions.text: What problem did Creative Commons solve for culture and education?

choices.text: It gave authors a standard, legally solid way to grant sharing permissions instead of copyright's all-or-nothing default
It made registering copyright cheaper
It required all creative work to be sold commercially

questions.explanation: Founded by Lessig and colleagues in 2001, CC did for creative work what the GPL did for code: standardized licenses (attribution, share-alike…) that make deliberate openness practical.

questions.text: What did the Budapest Open Access Initiative (2002) declare?

choices.text: That the internet made it possible for peer-reviewed knowledge to reach all curious minds — an unprecedented public good
That scientific journals should raise subscription prices
That research should circulate only among universities

questions.explanation: Open access answered the absurdity of publicly funded research locked behind paywalls. arXiv, PLOS and institutional repositories made the declaration real.

questions.text: According to Marcel Mauss's The Gift, how does a gift differ from a market sale?

choices.text: A sale closes the relationship; a gift keeps it open and points forward — pass it on
A gift always requires equal payment in return
There is no real difference; both are economic exchanges

questions.explanation: Mauss found gifts create relationships and obligations — to give, to receive, to reciprocate. Status in gift cultures flows to those who give well: the exact economy of free software and Wikipedia.

questions.text: Open Knowledge uses the highly permissive MIT license. What is the project's stated intent?

choices.text: The license is a floor, not a compass: the intent is open libraries given as gifts, not paywalled course products
The MIT license legally forbids commercial use
The license requires every library to charge for certificates

questions.explanation: MIT permits virtually everything — that is how tools spread. But the tradition Open Knowledge joins (Alexandria, the Encyclopédie, Carnegie, GNU, Wikipedia) points one way: give it away.

questions.text: What does 'the learner is not a product' mean in practice for Open Knowledge?

choices.text: No names, no emails, no profiles, no tracking — reading requires nothing but curiosity
Learners must pay to avoid advertising
Only registered users may access courses

questions.explanation: The public library ethic, ported to the web: free at the point of use, and discreet. Even in database mode, identities are pseudonymous and no personal data is requested.

questions.text: What is Open Knowledge's stance on AI-assisted course content?

choices.text: Welcome, always disclosed, and sources always credited — AI structures knowledge but must never erase where it came from
Forbidden in all courses
Allowed as long as it is kept secret from learners

questions.explanation: Courses carry an aiAssisted flag shown clearly to learners, and bibliographies credit sources. Transparency is part of the gift.
